strengths: Addresses genuinely important problems in video-to-audio generation: temporal synchronization, long-form capability, and few-step inference, each well-motivated with clear perceptual or practical justification

First application of shortcut loss to video-to-audio generation, enabling high-fidelity few-step sampling without distillation. Figure 5 demonstrates robustness with minimal degradation down to 8 steps while baselines degrade significantly

Comprehensive, well-designed evaluation combining multiple complementary metrics (FAD, KL divergence, IS, ImageBind, DeSync, SWSD) with proper human evaluation methodology (blind, randomized, 18 participants, A.3)

Novel combination of techniques for V2A: VideoPrism-based synchronization model with well-justified batch size constraints, masked flow matching for audio conditioning, and architecture modifications (MMDiT-X + DiT blocks) designed thoughtfully for multimodal fusion

Demonstrates practical capabilities beyond short-form: audio conditioning preserves spectral characteristics (Figure 4, Section A.2), long-form generation maintains quality to 60+ seconds, and iterative extension approach is validated quantitatively (Figure 5 right)

Transparent implementation details with sufficient specificity for reproducibility (A.4, A.5): architecture configurations, hyperparameters, training procedures, and honest discussion of limitations (audio quality gap, scene-change issues, model size disparity)
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty: individual components are primarily adaptations (flow matching from Liu et al. 2022, shortcut loss from Frans et al. 2025, masked objective from Chen et al. 2025/VampNet, VideoPrism backbone pre-existing). Unfair model comparison: SALSA-V is 643M parameters vs MMAudio's 1.03B (38% smaller). While acknowledged, this makes it unclear whether improvements stem from methods or reduced model capacity. No size-controlled ablation comparing equivalent model architectures

Mixed human evaluation results undermine core claims: while synchronization is superior (3.52 vs 2.92), overall quality lags MMAudio (3.43 vs 3.29). Some objective metrics favor MMAudio (KL_PANNs: 1.81 vs 1.77). Explanation that scaling would close the gap is untested

Long-form generation approach has fundamental limitations: relies on iterative inference-time prepending rather than architectural solution. Human evaluation scale insufficient for long-form claims: only 10 test videos, 18 participants, 180 total scores. Critically, all human evaluation samples are ≤10 seconds (short-form range). No human evaluation of actual long-form outputs (20-60s) or scene-transition robustness

Synchronization model training introduces potential circularity: filters large audio-visual dataset using their own synchronization model (>900h filtered), then uses learned features from same model in generative pipeline. Makes it difficult to isolate the synchronization model's contribution versus better-aligned training data

Batch size constraint on synchronization pretraining unexplored: finding that batch size >28 hurts features (Section 3.1) suggests fundamental scaling limitations, yet implications for larger datasets and industrial deployment not discussed

Reproducibility constraints limit practical adoption: requires TPU v4-8 infrastructure, proprietary studio Foley dataset, Panda70M filtering pipeline, and JAX conversions of multiple pretrained models. No code release mentioned

Missing technical justifications: cubic interpolation + learned upsampling for length unification (Eq. 4) not compared to alternatives; 43 Hz VAE sampling rate not ablated; 25% consistency target ratio not ablated; optional self-attention on first n blocks not ablated or justified

Well-motivated technical contributions addressing real limitations: (1) contrastive synchronization learning with smaller batches to avoid semantic alignment problem, (2) masked flow matching for audio conditioning and spectral style transfer, (3) long-form generation via iterative outpainting
